overview.body:
**Ratnasambhava** (*ratnasambhava*) — Jewel-Born, South · 'Born of the Jewel' — the Dhyānibuddha of the southern jewel family — belongs to the Buddhist tradition, where it is catalogued under the domain "Jewel-Born, South". The name means "'Born of the Jewel' — the Dhyānibuddha of the southern jewel family".

**Ratnasambhava** is jewel-born, south. The name means "'Born of the Jewel' — the Dhyānibuddha of the southern jewel family" and belongs to the buddhist tradition.

PuniCodex restores the name as **Ratnasambhava** and serves its temple at [its temple](https://punicodex.com/ratnasambhava/). The restoration needs no distinctive letters or diacritics its ASCII form would lose, which places the name in Tier 2. The plain ASCII form *ratnasambhava* survives as a modern convenience imposed by the early domain-name system; the restoration, not the fallback, is the form the project defends as philologically complete.

the-name.body:
The name is attested in Devanagari as **रत्नसम्भव**. Etymologically it means "'Born of the Jewel' — the Dhyānibuddha of the southern jewel family".

The ASCII form *ratnasambhava* survives only because the early domain-name system could not carry diacritics; it is a technological compromise, not an ancient spelling. The Unicode restoration **Ratnasambhava** recovers the full diacritic detail of the scholarly transliteration directly in the address bar. The restoration needs no distinctive letters or diacritics its ASCII form would lose, which places the name in Tier 2.

pronunciation.body:
The reconstructed pronunciation of the name is **/ratnasambhava/** — Restored scholarly form.

Phoneme by phoneme:

- **ratnasambhava** — The canonical restored form Ratnasambhava.

For the modern speaker, the closest approximation is: Say "ratnasambhava" with the stress and length implied by the scholarly restoration "Ratnasambhava".

The ASCII form "ratnasambhava" is a DNS compromise; the restoration "Ratnasambhava" preserves the name's scholarly dignity.

The pronunciation given above reconstructs the sound world in which Ratnasambhava was invoked. Modern speakers should not expect exact identity with ancient phonology; the reconstruction is a scholarly compass, not a performance prescription. The restoration Ratnasambhava keeps the prosodic information visible even when the name is typed in plain ASCII.

original-script.body:
The name is preserved in Devanagari as **रत्नसम्भव**.[^1]

The scholarly transliteration is *Ratnasambhava*.

The rendering proceeds step by step:

- Sanskrit Ratnasambhava is written in Devanagari as रत्नसम्भव
- IAST transliteration maps each Devanagari vowel and consonant to a Latin equivalent
- Macrons mark long vowels (ā, ī, ū); dots beneath consonants mark retroflex articulation (ṭ, ḍ, ṇ, ṣ)

mythology.body:
The stories of Ratnasambhava place jewel-born, south at the center of a living mythological world.

### Origins (Myth)

Ratnasambhava appears in buddhist tradition as jewel-born, south. The name's meaning, "'Born of the Jewel' — the Dhyānibuddha of the southern jewel family", shapes the narratives told about this figure.

### Worship and Memory (Cult)

Devotees and later tradition-keepers preserved Ratnasambhava in ritual, text, and iconography, ensuring the name survived into the modern scholarly record.

The myths of Ratnasambhava survive in fragments, summaries, and later retellings. Each version reflects the interests of its tellers — poets, priests, philosophers, and scholars. The PuniCodex entry does not privilege a single version; it gathers the attestations so that readers can compare them. The restoration Ratnasambhava gives the figure a stable name around which these variants orbit.

syncretism.body:
Within the Buddhist tradition, closely related names in the corpus include [[akshobhya|Akṣobhya]], [[amitabha|Amitābha]], [[amoghasiddhi|Amoghasiddhi]], [[arhat|Arhat]], [[asanga|Asanga]], and [[avalokiteshvara|Avalokiteśvara]].

Cross-cultural identifications are rarely one-to-one. Ratnasambhava may be likened to figures in neighboring traditions without being identical to them. The PuniCodex crosslink index records these resonances as relationships, not equations. The restored form Ratnasambhava makes such comparisons possible across language boundaries.

cultural-legacy.body:
Ratnasambhava remains a touchstone for understanding buddhist religion, art, and identity.

The modern afterlife of Ratnasambhava includes scholarly editions, artistic adaptations, and popular references. Each reuse renegotiates the figure’s meaning for a new audience. The PuniCodex temple participates in that afterlife by ensuring that the restored name Ratnasambhava remains findable and citable.

archaeology.body:
No monument, inscription, or artifact in the current PuniCodex corpus is yet assigned to Ratnasambhava with certainty. That absence should be read honestly: for a Buddhist name of this type the material record is expected to be thin, and the primary evidence remains the textual testimony gathered in the Scholarly Sources section.

Were such evidence to surface, it would take recognizable forms: votive or dedicatory inscriptions naming रत्नसम्भव, sanctuary or cult remains tied to jewel-born and iconography matching its traditional attributes (name and domain). Each candidate would be weighed against the reconstructed form of the name before entering the scholarly record.

meditation.body:
To contemplate Ratnasambhava is to hold the idea of jewel-Born, South in the mind and to ask what of it endures. The name means "'Born of the Jewel' — the Dhyānibuddha of the southern jewel family" — and a name that carries its meaning so openly invites meditation rather than mere recollection. The tradition remembers the name as jewel-Born, South · 'Born of the Jewel' — the Dhyānibuddha of the southern jewel family.

Sit with the restored form — Ratnasambhava — and the diacritics themselves become the practice: each mark is a small act of attention, a refusal to let the plain ASCII form *ratnasambhava* stand in for the whole. What the tradition preserved in this name, the restoration asks the reader to preserve in turn.

pali-canon.body:
The Pāli Canon preserves the earliest stratum of Buddhist scripture in Middle Indic. While Ratnasambhava often belongs to later Mahāyāna elaboration, the canonical values of mindfulness, compassion, and liberation underpin the figure's significance.

The restoration Ratnasambhava follows IAST convention used in Buddhist studies.

mahayana-sutras.body:
Mahāyāna sūtras expand the cult of Ratnasambhava across Sanskrit, Chinese, and Tibetan transmissions. Texts such as the Lotus Sūtra, Avataṃsaka, and Pure Land sūtras place the figure in expansive cosmologies of buddhahood and bodhisattva activity.

The IAST form Ratnasambhava marks the Sanskrit reconstruction behind those transmissions.

Buddhist commentaries — Śākyamitra, Vasubandhu, and later Tibetan and East Asian exegetes — systematize the mythology and practice surrounding Ratnasambhava. These texts connect the name to rituals, visualizations, and doctrinal categories.

The restoration Ratnasambhava serves as the stable scholarly anchor across languages and schools.
